title: Productive State-Space Exploration for Multi-turn RL in LLM Agents

paper.title: Productive State-Space Exploration for Multi-turn RL in LLM Agents
paper.abstract:
Abstract Reinforcement Learning (RL) for Large Language Model (LLM) agents in multi-turn, long-horizon environments remains challenging due to inefficient action selection and repetitive behavioral patterns. In particular, agents often become trapped in high-confidence yet unproductive behaviors, repeatedly executing invalid actions or entering action loops that hinder task completion. We observe that these frequently violate environment preconditions, revealing a mismatch between the agent’s representation of the internal state and the dynamics of the underlying environment. In addition, repetitive high-confidence actions lead to cyclical behaviors that provide little to no progress towards the goal.
We argue that addressing these challenges requires more productive task-aligned exploration to improve the agent’s understanding of environment dynamics. Motivated by intrinsic curiosity-driven exploration, we propose a conditional state-space exploration framework that balances task completion with intrinsic information-seeking behavior. Specifically, we introduce an intrinsic reward that penalizes actions whose observation duplicates prior state memory. This provides the benefit of reducing redundant behaviors and encouraging state-space coverage without relying on a general information-theoretic measure. Strong experimental results demonstrate that our approach substantially improves policy learning in multi-turn environments, mitigating invalid actions and repetitive loops.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Reinforcement learning (RL) has become an important training paradigm for large language model (LLM) agents that must operate over multiple turns in partially observable, long-horizon environments ( Carta et al., 2023 ; Shani et al., 2024 ; Guan et al., 2026 ) . In contrast to single-step prediction tasks, these agents must select actions sequentially, update internal memory, and adapt to changing states while receiving sparse and delayed feedback. Recent work has shown that RL is increasingly relevant for improving reasoning, agentic control, and long-horizon decision making in LLMs, but it has also revealed a persistent difficulty: agents often become stuck in repetitive, high-confidence behaviors that are locally plausible yet unproductive for the task ( Liu et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2025 ; Xi et al., 2025 ) . In such settings, effective learning depends not only on exploiting promising actions but also on exploring the environment in a way that improves the agent’s understanding of its dynamics. In practice, agents often overcommit to high-confidence actions that are locally plausible but globally unhelpful, leading to invalid interactions or repetitive loops that consume budget without advancing the task. Such failures, as shown in Figure 1 , typically reflect a mismatch between the agent’s internal state representation and the true environment dynamics, especially when the agent lacks sufficient feedback about which actions are feasible or informative. This motivates the need for a form of productive state-space exploration that helps the agent learn environment dynamics while remaining aligned with task completion. Figure 1: Failure modes of an RL-trained LLM agent in ALFWorld . (a) Repetitive action loop. The agent repeats an invalid action and receives the same failure feedback until the step budget runs out. (b) Repetitive reasoning loop. The agent’s reasoning ignores the current observation, and the agent cycles between the fridge and the microwave without completing the task. In both cases the agent’s internal state diverges from the environment dynamics, and the looping steps consume interaction budget while revealing no new observation. These are the steps our intrinsic reward penalizes. A natural way to improve exploration is to encourage the agent to visit a broader range of states. In principle, increasing the entropy of the explored state space can improve coverage, reduce mode collapse, and expose the agent to more informative trajectories. However, directly maximizing exploration entropy can also be problematic. If encouraged too strongly, the agent may drift toward diverse but task-irrelevant behavior, thereby sacrificing progress on the underlying objective. In long-horizon environments, this tension between exploration and exploitation is especially important: exploration should broaden the agent’s experience, but it should not pull the policy away from useful action sequences that lead to task completion. This paper pursues productive exploration through intrinsic curiosity-driven rewards , with a conservative formulation that preserves task alignment. Rather than positively rewarding state-space entropy increase, we penalize any step whose observation has already appeared in the episode. The intuition is that unhelpful actions, such as invalid steps or redundant repetitions, consume interaction budget and policy probability without revealing anything new about the environment. They can be detected simply by checking whether each new observation adds any new information to the agent’s memory. Our formulation reframes entropy increase as a consequence of avoiding unproductive actions rather than as an objective to be optimized directly. The penalty improves within-episode state-space coverage, while the task reward keeps exploration tied to task completion. We further formalize this argument by showing that the cumulative penalty measures how many distinct observations an episode visits, and that it bounds the episode’s visitation entropy (Section 3 ). A single-step analysis further shows that novel observations always increase entropy, while revisits of frequent observations decrease it. Our approach is consistent with the broader literature on intrinsic motivation in reinforcement learning, where curiosity, novelty seeking, and uncertainty reduction have been used to improve learning under sparse rewards Chentanez et al. (2004) ; Aubret et al. (2019) ; Gao et al. (2025) . It also aligns with recent efforts to train long-horizon LLM agents, where robustness depends not only on reasoning ability but also on the capacity to avoid repetitive or uninformative interactions with the environment Kalyan and Andrews (2025) . Within this setting, penalizing unhelpful actions provides a simple compromise between unrestricted entropy maximization and overly conservative exploitation. The resulting behavior promotes broader state coverage without losing contact with the task. In summary, we propose a conditional intrinsic reward framework that supports productive exploration by penalizing actions that yield no new informative observation. Our key argument is that entropy expansion is useful, but only when it is induced indirectly through the suppression of redundant or uninformative behavior. This allows the agent to explore more broadly while maintaining a strong coupling to task progress. We evaluate our proposed exploration strategy on two prominent multi-turn benchmark environments: ALFWorld and WebShop . Empirical results show that our approach surpasses recent baselines in performance metrics of success rates and significantly mitigates both invalid and repetitive action rates.

sections.heading: 2.1 Prompting-Based LLM Agents
sections.text: Early LLM agent frameworks rely on prompting for multi-step reasoning and action selection without updating model weights. ReAct Yao et al. (2023) interleaves reasoning (Thought) and actions (Act), outperforming pure reasoning or action prompting on tasks such as ALFWorld and WebShop. Reflexion Shinn et al. (2023) extends this with verbal reinforcement, storing self-reflections from failed episodes in episodic memory to guide future decisions. Although ReAct and Reflexion improve performance on multi-turn tasks, both methods depend heavily on self-evaluation quality, which degrades for smaller LLMs, and cannot structurally suppress invalid actions since prompting alone cannot alter action priors.

sections.heading: 2.2 Reinforcement Learning for LLM Agents
sections.text: Recently, reinforcement learning (RL) has emerged as a principled approach for post-training LLMs, with growing focus on agent-based LLMs in multi-turn environments. PPO Schulman et al. (2017) and its critic-free variant GRPO Shao et al. (2024) , which estimates baselines from group rollout scores, are widely adopted for RL-based LLM training. RLOO Kool et al. (2019) ; Ahmadian et al. (2024) further reduces variance without a learned critic, and AGILE Feng et al. (2024) applies PPO to LLM agents using a four-module architecture with proactive expert consultation, significantly outperforming prompting on long-horizon QA tasks. Retrospex Xiang et al. (2024) combines an offline RL critic with LLM action likelihood through dynamic rescoring, improving performance on ALFWorld and WebShop over prompting baselines. GiGPO Feng et al. (2025) captures global trajectory quality and group-level effectiveness without additional rollouts, providing rich signals for LLM agent learning. Recently, ProxMO Fang et al. (2026) presents a framework to address GRPO’s context-agnostic normalization and GiGPO’s discrete state-grouping limitation. They explore the provision of gradient intensities based on task difficulty, and replace hard boundary partitioning with continuous semantic similarity weighting, so as to provide richer reward signals that are less task-agnostic. In totality, these works establish multiple avenues to improve vanilla RL for multi-turn LLM agents, such as stable baselines and supporting tools to provide more information about the world. However, they do not directly address the exploration failure modes we identify in this work. Specifically, we explore the notion of invalid actions that arise from environment precondition mismatches, resulting in action loops driven by high-confidence but unproductive behaviors. Our approach adds a conditional intrinsic reward that explicitly penalizes such behaviors during RL training. Recent RL methods for multi-turn LLM agents focus on improving credit assignment, exploration, and training stability. ArCHer Zhou and Zanette (2024) introduces a hierarchical RL framework combining off-policy temporal difference learning at the utterance level with on-policy policy gradients at the token level, substantially improving sample efficiency over PPO while emphasizing information-seeking behavior in multi-turn settings. Tree-GRPO Ji et al. (2026) improves training efficiency by replacing chain-based rollouts with tree-structured sampling, enabling step-level supervision from outcome rewards alone. Addressing exploration instability, EPO Xu et al. (2025) identifies exploration-exploitation cascade failure in shared multi-turn policies and mitigates it via trajectory-level entropy regularization and entropy smoothing, yielding gains on ScienceWorld and ALFWorld. Similarly, RAGEN Wang et al. (2025) studies multi-turn RL failure modes, identifying an “Echo Trap” caused by reward variance cliffs and gradient spikes, and proposes trajectory filtering with a critic for stabilization. While these works improve how agents learn—through efficient credit propagation, entropy stabilization, or robust optimization—our approach is complementary, focusing on what to explore by penalizing invalid or repetitive actions that fail to expand state-space knowledge, without itself performing credit assignment across turns.

sections.heading: 2.3 Intrinsic Motivation and Exploration in RL
sections.text: Intrinsic motivation has long been used to improve exploration under sparse rewards by encouraging state diversity and novelty. Curiosity-based methods like Pathak et al. (2017) ; Burda et al. (2019) reward novel states or high prediction errors, while count-based exploration formalizes revisitation penalties through information gain via KL-divergence between prior and posterior state beliefs ( Bellemare et al., 2016 ) . Extending state-entropy exploration to task-reward settings, Kim et al. (2023) propose value-conditional state entropy (VCSE), addressing the tendency of naive entropy maximization to overexplore low-value regions by maximizing entropy within value partitions. Mutti et al. (2021) ; Ashlag et al. (2025) further provide a theoretical foundation for state entropy regularization, showing that it improves robustness and promotes broader coverage across multiple viable trajectories, unlike policy entropy which mainly injects noise along a dominant path. These works motivate our approach – by targeting state-space entropy, our conditional intrinsic penalty discourages revisiting already-observed states. Additionally, by tying the penalty to information gain rather than raw visitation counts, we ensure that only transitions that fail to expand the agent’s knowledge are penalized, preserving the pull of the task reward toward goal-relevant states. In LLM-based RL, intrinsic signals have recently been explored to complement sparse task rewards. MIRA Nourzad and Joe-Wong (2026) improves exploration by using memory graphs from agent trajectories and semantic reasoning to shape PPO advantages, mitigating poor early critic calibration. Similarly, our approach leverages accumulated experience for exploration, but instead defines an information-gain-based intrinsic signal that penalizes observations failing to expand state knowledge. This is simpler to compute, and is motivated by Shannon entropy (Proposition 2 ), while being aligned with repetitive and invalid behaviors in text-based environments. Further recent work on moral intrinsic rewards Tennant et al. (2025) has shown that intrinsic signals can shape agent behavior toward desired norms without task-specific reward engineering, reinforcing the broader applicability of intrinsic motivation for LLM alignment. Our contribution fits within this emerging direction: intrinsic rewards as a practical mechanism for shaping LLM agent behavior in ways that extrinsic rewards alone cannot achieve.

sections.heading: 3.1 Problem Setup
sections.text: We consider reinforcement learning for LLM agents operating in partially observable, long-horizon interactive environments. At each timestep t t , the agent is in state s t s_{t} , takes an action a t ∈ 𝒜 a_{t}\in\mathcal{A} , and receives an observation o t o_{t} from the environment. We define the agent’s state s t s_{t} as the set of all observations received so far along the trajectory, i.e., the information the agent has accumulated about the environment up to time t t . The objective is to learn a policy π ⁡ ( a t ∣ s t ) \pi(a_{t}\mid s_{t}) that maximizes expected cumulative reward while completing the task within a finite horizon T T . Unlike standard short-horizon decision problems, this setting introduces two recurring failure modes. First, the agent may produce invalid actions whose preconditions are not satisfied, causing the transition to fail or yielding no meaningful progress. Second, the agent may enter action loops , repeatedly selecting a small set of actions that do not improve task state or move the agent closer to completion. Both issues reduce learning efficiency and often reflect an imperfect internal model of the environment dynamics. In practice, these failures are especially harmful in LLM agents because they waste interaction budget and reinforce unproductive behavior patterns.

sections.heading: 3.2 State Representation
sections.text: To support long-horizon decision making, we define the agent’s state as the accumulated observation history: s t = { o 1 , o 2 , … , o t } . s_{t}=\{o_{1},o_{2},\dots,o_{t}\}. This representation captures the information available to the agent at time t t . Instead of relying only on the most recent observation, the agent maintains a memory of the full trajectory of unique observations , enabling it to reason about what has already been explored and what remains uncertain. This accumulated state serves as the basis for evaluating whether a new observation provides additional information about the environment. At each step, the agent observes the current state s t s_{t} , selects an action a t a_{t} , and receives the next observation o t + 1 o_{t+1} . The state is then updated by appending the new observation: s t + 1 = s t ∪ { o t + 1 } . s_{t+1}=s_{t}\cup\{o_{t+1}\}. The intrinsic reward is computed from the change in information content between s t s_{t} and o t + 1 o_{t+1} . If the new observation does not improve the agent’s knowledge of the environment, a negative intrinsic reward is assigned. This signal is combined with the task reward and used to update the policy.

sections.heading: How Does the Penalty Teach Preconditions?
sections.text: Let ℱ ⁡ ( s ) \mathcal{F}(s) be the set of actions whose preconditions fail in state s s . We assume that (A1) every a ∈ ℱ ⁡ ( s ) a\in\mathcal{F}(s) returns the same observation o ⊥ o_{\bot} , independent of a a and s s , and (A2) a failed action leaves the state unchanged. Under A1, every precondition violation after the first in an episode yields o t + 1 = o ⊥ ∈ s t o_{t+1}=o_{\bot}\in s_{t} and is penalized, whichever action failed. The policy is thus pushed away from all precondition-violating actions, not only from repeating one. Under A2, avoiding them loses no information, so the penalty does not conflict with information gathering.

sections.heading: 3.4 Final Reward
sections.text: The final reward used for policy optimization combines the task reward and the intrinsic reward: r t = r t task + λ ​ r t intrinsic , r_{t}=r_{t}^{\text{task}}+\lambda r_{t}^{\text{intrinsic}}, where λ ≥ 0 \lambda\geq 0 balances task performance and exploration pressure. The resulting objective is J ⁡ ( π ) = 𝔼 π ​ [ ∑ t = 0 T − 1 ρ t ​ r t ] , J(\pi)=\mathbb{E}_{\pi}\left[\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\rho^{t}r_{t}\right], where ρ ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] \rho\in[0,1] is the discount factor. This objective encourages the agent to maximize task reward while avoiding actions that fail to improve state-space coverage.

An overly strong incentive for novelty may lead the policy to explore diverse but irrelevant trajectories. By contrast, penalizing non-informative actions creates a task-constrained pressure toward visiting more distinct observations within an episode. The policy is discouraged from remaining in low-diversity action cycles, but it is still constrained by the external task reward, which ensures that exploration remains useful for task completion. This conditional structure is especially important in long-horizon environments, where the agent must balance exploration and exploitation over many sequential decisions. Actions that expand state coverage or contribute to task progress receive no intermediate positive incentive. However, actions that actively fail to improve the agent’s state knowledge are penalized . As a result, the learned policy is pushed toward trajectories that are both diverse and productive. This penalization mechanism encourages productive exploration by discouraging repeated observations and promoting broader coverage of the agent’s experience. sections.heading: 4.1 Baselines
sections.text: For the performance comparison, we benchmark against several state-of-the-art recent baseline models. These include prompting frameworks and those trained with RL. The prompting baselines are Gemini-2.5 Team et al. (2023) , GPT-4o Achiam et al. (2023) , Qwen-2.5 ( Qwen et al., 2025 ) , ReAct ( Yao et al., 2023 ) and Reflexion ( Shinn et al., 2023 ) frameworks. The RL trained baselines include PPO Schulman et al. (2017) , RLOO Kool et al. (2019) ; Ahmadian et al. (2024) , GRPO Shao et al. (2024) , GiGPO Feng et al. (2025) , ProxMO Fang et al. (2026) . The most recent and relevant baselines for our approach are GiGPO and ProxMO, since we aim to address challenges in multi-turn LLM agent training with RL. We do not re-run these baselines, all Table 1 numbers except our method are quoted from their original publications. For the additional analyses (Table 3 , Sections 4.4 – 4.5 and Appendix A.2 ), we re-train GiGPO with the latest official verl-agent implementation, without the intrinsic penalty, and evaluate it under exactly the same protocol as our agent.

sections.heading: 4.2 Training Details:
sections.text: We train Qwen-2.5-1.5B-Instruct model with the proposed state-space exploration rewards along with Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) based RL training. We run all our experiments on top of verl-agent framework released by GiGPO Feng et al. (2025) . We train for 300 steps with all other hyperparameters kept same as in the framework. We set the maximum steps at 50 for ALFWorld and 15 for WebShop as with GiGPO. The strength of state-space exploration penalty, γ \gamma , as defined in Equation 1 , is set 1 40 \frac{1}{40} of the final success reward. Full reproducibility details ( γ \gamma selection, reward normalization, splits) are in Appendix A.3 . Compared to GiGPO, our method achieves consistent gains across all ALFWorld subtasks, improving the overall success rate from 86.7 % 86.7\% to 94.0 % 94.0\% . The improvements are particularly pronounced on challenging long-horizon tasks such as Cool ( + 7.6 % +7.6\% ) and Pick2 ( + 7.5 % +7.5\% ), indicating stronger sequential reasoning and more effective action planning. Compared to ProxMO, a recent proximity-based multi-turn optimization framework designed for practical credit assignment in LLM agent training, our approach still achieves better overall performance across both benchmarks. Specifically, it improves the overall ALFWorld success rate from 90.6 % 90.6\% to 94.0 % 94.0\% , while increasing the WebShop success rate from 67.1 % 67.1\% to 78.3 % 78.3\% . sections.heading: 4.4 Intrinsic Productive Exploration
sections.text: To look beyond overall success rates, we evaluate the behavioral dynamics of our agent against the competitive baseline GiGPO ( Feng et al., 2025 ) . This analysis focuses on intrinsic productive exploration - the agent’s capacity to autonomously discover optimal state-action trajectories through targeted, purposeful environment interactions, rather than wasting computational steps on redundant or unproductive behaviors. We define three behavioral diagnostics across the ALFWorld and WebShop benchmarks to quantify the efficiency and productivity of the agent’s intrinsic exploration strategy: • Mean Episode Length: The average number of sequential steps to complete a task instance. • Invalid Action Rate: The frequency of actions that fail (violate action preconditions). It is detected as described in Appendix A.3 . • Repetitive Action Rate: The frequency of steps spent executing identical actions. We consider an action repetitive when either the action or the resulting observation is repeated in the trajectory. The empirical results detailing these behavioral metrics are shown in Table 2 . In ALFWorld , our method compresses the Mean Episode Length from ≈ 32 \approx 32 steps down to ≈ 22 \approx 22 relative to GiGPO. Similar trend persists in the WebShop , where the gains are not as profound as in ALFWorld , however help in score improvement compared to GiGPO. More broadly, the results suggest: • Learning of Environment Dynamics: The improvement in Mean Episode Length and Invalid Action Rate shows that the agent better understands the environment dynamics and, in particular, rarely repeats actions that have already failed. • Loop Resolution and Novelty Seeking: The most supporting evidence of productive exploration is revealed by the Repetitive Action Rate in ALFWorld . While GiGPO spends 45.31 % 45.31\% of its execution trajectory repeating identical commands, our approach drops this rate dramatically to 11.53 % 11.53\% . This absolute reduction of 33.78 % 33.78\% demonstrates that our intrinsic penalty inherently disincentivizes stale, repeated states. Instead, it forces the agent to continuously break out of loops and seek novel, progressive environmental interactions. Both the above inferences can also be seen in qualitative action trajectories as shown in Figure 2 . The contrast in the decrease in the number of invalid actions relative to Figure 1 suggests our approach of penalizing actions which repeat states is indeed helpful in reducing the redundancy of the agent’s trajectory. To examine information gathering more closely, we record every step of our agent and of the re-trained GiGPO agent (Section 4.1 ). Our agent searches the partially observable environment more widely while wasting fewer steps: it visits more distinct locations, revisits fewer of them, obtains new information from a larger share of its information-gathering actions, and finds the target object more often. The two agents also fail differently. GiGPO’s failed episodes are dominated by repeated observations, whereas ours keep exploring new states until the step budget runs out. These advantages hold on both seen and unseen scenes. Per action, both agents satisfy preconditions for nearly all of their actions; our agent’s advantage lies in avoiding repeated failures rather than in avoiding a first one (Appendix A.2 ).

sections.heading: 4.5 Effect of the Intrinsic Penalty on Exploration
sections.text: To isolate the effect of the penalty, we train two PPO agents from the same base model with identical settings, differing only in the penalty weight ( γ = 0 \gamma=0 vs. γ = 1 40 \gamma=\frac{1}{40} of the success reward), and evaluate them after 100 training steps (details in Appendix A.2 ). We measure exploration by the duplicate-observation rate (steps whose observation repeats an earlier one), the location revisit rate ( go to actions to an already visited location), the new-information rate (information-gathering actions go to , open and examine that reveal a new observation), and whether the target object is ever observed. A precondition violation is an executed action outside the environment’s admissible set; we report violations after the first one in an episode and the recovery rate, i.e. how often the action following a violation is admissible. The penalty broadens exploration during training. Starting from identical behavior, the penalized agent reduces repeated observations much faster and covers a substantially larger part of the state space (Figure 3 ). This broader exploration precedes its gain in success, which emerges after the first 50 steps. The learned policy explores productively at test time. It repeats observations and revisits locations far less often, gains new information from more of its actions, and finds the target object more often, equally on seen and unseen scenes (Table 4 ). Better exploration leads to better use of feedback and higher success. Since repeated failures reveal nothing new, the penalized agent makes far fewer repeated precondition violations, recovers more often, satisfies preconditions more often, and succeeds considerably more often on both splits. sections.heading: 5 Conclusion
sections.text: In this paper, we addressed the tendency of RL-trained LLM agent policies to repeat invalid actions and fall into action loops in multi-turn, long-horizon environments. We introduced a conditional state-space exploration framework driven by an information-aware intrinsic reward. Instead of directly maximizing unconstrained state entropy, which risks driving the agent toward task-irrelevant trajectories, our approach reframes exploration by penalizing actions that produce redundant state information. Our experimental evaluation demonstrates that this framework achieves substantial performance gains and significantly mitigates action repetition and circular reasoning patterns.

sections.heading: Limitations
sections.text: Our experiments are conducted primarily on smaller reasoning models. Because exploration strategies are inherently influenced by a model’s overall capacity and pre-trained priors, larger instruction-tuned models may exhibit fewer failures than those documented in this study. Growth in model scale often mitigates baseline reasoning bottlenecks; nevertheless, optimizing smaller models remains highly valuable. Enhancing the capabilities of these smaller architectures enables more practical, targeted applications, particularly in hardware-constrained environments where deployment efficiency is critical. Additionally, this work focuses specifically on text-based environments within ALFWorld and WebShop, which feature relatively small, well-defined action spaces that lend themselves well to set representations. Environments with larger, continuous, or stochastic action spaces may exhibit vastly different dynamics under this set-based state representation, potentially limiting direct generalizability. Regardless of these limitations, our approach provides a structurally sound framework for agent reasoning and state representation in multi-turn settings. Ultimately, the insights gained from our set-based representation and reward design establish a foundation for future scaling and adaptation across more complex, open-ended environments.

sections.heading: ALFWorld.
sections.text: ALFWorld ( Shridhar et al., 2020 ) is a text-based interactive environment designed for studying embodied decision making and long-horizon reasoning in language agents. Derived from the ALFRED benchmark, it converts household manipulation tasks into a partially observable textual setting where agents interact through natural language actions and observations. Tasks typically involve navigation, object manipulation, and sequential planning over multiple turns, making the environment particularly suitable for evaluating reinforcement learning methods for LLM agents under sparse rewards and delayed feedback. Concretely, ALFWorld contains 6 task types of various difficulty. The tasks are: • Pick & Place: agent must find an object of a specified type, pick it up, find the correct location to place it, and place it down there. • Examine in Light: agent must find an object of a specified type, locate and turn on a light source with the object still in hand. • Clean & Place: agent must find an object of a specified type, pick it up, move to a sink or a basin, turn on the faucet and wash the object, find the correct location to place it, and place it down there. • Heat & Place: agent must find an object of a specified type, pick it up, move to the microwave, heat the object by turning on the microwave, find the correct location to place it, and place it down there. • Cool & Place: agent must find an object of a specified type, pick it up, move to the fridge, place the object in the fridge to cool it, find the correct location to place it, and place it down there. • Pick Two & Place: agent must find an object of a specified type, find the correct location to place it, place it down there, look for another object of a specified type, pick up the object, return to the previous location, place it down there together with the first object.

sections.heading: WebShop.
sections.text: WebShop ( Yao et al., 2022 ) is an e-commerce interaction benchmark that evaluates language agents on realistic online shopping tasks. In this environment, agents must search through large collections of products, inspect item descriptions and reviews, and iteratively refine decisions to satisfy user instructions. Unlike embodied environments, WebShop emphasizes retrieval, preference understanding, and multi-step reasoning in semi-structured web settings. The benchmark is widely used for evaluating the effectiveness of sequential decision-making and reinforcement learning approaches for interactive LLM agents. Concretely, the WebShop dataset contains 1,000,000 products, 670 unique attributes, 842,849 unique options, extracted publicly from Amazon. It presents over 12,000 annotated trajectories and an action space of 8 valid actions.

sections.heading: A.2 Additional Experiments
sections.text: This subsection reports additional ALFWorld experiments that analyze (i) whether the trained agent gathers information more effectively at test time, and (ii) whether more of its actions satisfy their preconditions. Sections 4.4 and 4.5 summarize the main findings; here we give the full results.

sections.heading: Setup.
sections.text: We compare our agent with a GiGPO agent that we trained ourselves using the released verl-agent code. Both agents play the same 128 evaluation episodes (91 distinct games) from the ALFWorld in-distribution split, with sampling temperature 0.4 and at most 50 steps. We record every step (observation, admissible actions, chosen action and next observation) and compute all metrics below per episode, then average over episodes.

sections.heading: Test-time exploration and information gathering.

sections.heading: Repeated precondition violations.
sections.text: In ALFWorld , every action whose preconditions are not satisfied returns the same fixed observation, "Nothing happens." (Appendix A.3 ). The first violation in an episode therefore adds a new observation to the state memory and is not penalized, while every later violation in the same episode repeats this observation and is penalized. The penalty is thus not expected to prevent a first, exploratory violation, but to discourage the agent from violating preconditions again after it has already received this feedback. Table 7 measures this behavior on the same 128 episodes, using the following definitions: • Violation: an executed action that is not in the admissible set of the state in which it is taken, i.e. an action whose preconditions are not satisfied. we report violations after the first, which are the violations which receive the intrinsic penalty. Per episode divides their number by the 128 episodes. • Exact repeat of a failed action: a violation in which the agent executes the very same action string that has already failed earlier in the same episode. • Share of all violations: the percentage of an agent’s violations that fall into the given category. • Back-to-back violations: violations that immediately follow another violation. • Recovery after a violation: the percentage of violations whose next action is admissible. Our agent is less likely to violate preconditions again once it has received the failure feedback: it has fewer violations after the first in an episode. The clearest difference is in exact repeats. About half of GiGPO’s violations re-execute an action that has already failed in the same episode, compared with about a quarter of ours. Our agent also recovers more often, with the action following a violation more frequently being admissible. This pattern matches the mechanism of the penalty, which leaves the first violation unpenalized but penalizes repeating it. sections.heading: Relation to Proposition 2 .
sections.text: Proposition 2 bounds the visitation entropy H ⁡ ( P L ) H(P_{L}) of an episode by its number of duplicate observations D D . sections.heading: Invalid actions:
sections.text: The two environments signal invalid actions differently. In ALFWorld , every action whose preconditions are not satisfied returns the fixed observation "Nothing happens." , and we count a step as invalid when its observation matches this string or when the agent’s output contains no well-formed action. WebShop provides no failure message: an action that is not available on the current page, such as clicking an element that is not displayed, is ignored, and the environment returns the unchanged page. For WebShop , we therefore count a step as invalid when the agent’s output contains no well-formed action. Because an ignored action returns the same page, it always produces a duplicate observation and is penalized by our intrinsic reward.

Learn more × Back to arXiv License: CC BY 4.0 arXiv:2610.25957v1 [cs.AI] 19 Oct 2026 Productive State-Space Exploration for Multi-turn RL in LLM Agents Mohammed Haroon Dupty † Affiliation: Institute of Advanced Computing Affiliation: and Intelligence, A*STAR Email: haroon@u.nus.edu Yong Liang Goh Affiliation: Grabtaxi Holdings Pte Ltd Email: gyl@u.nus.edu Song Guo Affiliation: The Hong Kong University of Affiliation: Science and Technology Email: songguo@cse.ust.hk Wee Sun Lee Affiliation: School of Computing, Affiliation: National University of Singapore Email: leews@comp.nus.edu.sg Abstract Reinforcement Learning (RL) for Large Language Model (LLM) agents in multi-turn, long-horizon environments remains challenging due to inefficient action selection and repetitive behavioral patterns. In particular, agents often become trapped in high-confidence yet unproductive behaviors, repeatedly executing invalid actions or entering action loops that hinder task completion. We observe that these frequently violate environment preconditions, revealing a mismatch between the agent’s representation of the internal state and the dynamics of the underlying environment. In addition, repetitive high-confidence actions lead to cyclical behaviors that provide little to no progress towards the goal. We argue that addressing these challenges requires more productive task-aligned exploration to improve the agent’s understanding of environment dynamics. Motivated by intrinsic curiosity-driven exploration, we propose a conditional state-space exploration framework that balances task completion with intrinsic information-seeking behavior. Specifically, we introduce an intrinsic reward that penalizes actions whose observation duplicates prior state memory. This provides the benefit of reducing redundant behaviors and encouraging state-space coverage without relying on a general information-theoretic measure. Strong experimental results demonstrate that our approach substantially improves policy learning in multi-turn environments, mitigating invalid actions and repetitive loops. † † footnotetext: † Major part of this work was done while at the National University of Singapore. 1 Introduction Reinforcement learning (RL) has become an important training paradigm for large language model (LLM) agents that must operate over multiple turns in partially observable, long-horizon environments ( Carta et al., 2023 ; Shani et al., 2024 ; Guan et al., 2026 ) . In contrast to single-step prediction tasks, these agents must select actions sequentially, update internal memory, and adapt to changing states while receiving sparse and delayed feedback. Recent work has shown that RL is increasingly relevant for improving reasoning, agentic control, and long-horizon decision making in LLMs, but it has also revealed a persistent difficulty: agents often become stuck in repetitive, high-confidence behaviors that are locally plausible yet unproductive for the task ( Liu et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2025 ; Xi et al., 2025 ) . In such settings, effective learning depends not only on exploiting promising actions but also on exploring the environment in a way that improves the agent’s understanding of its dynamics. In practice, agents often overcommit to high-confidence actions that are locally plausible but globally unhelpful, leading to invalid interactions or repetitive loops that consume budget without advancing the task. Such failures, as shown in Figure 1 , typically reflect a mismatch between the agent’s internal state representation and the true environment dynamics, especially when the agent lacks sufficient feedback about which actions are feasible or informative. This motivates the need for a form of productive state-space exploration that helps the agent learn environment dynamics while remaining aligned with task completion. Figure 1: Failure modes of an RL-trained LLM agent in ALFWorld . (a) Repetitive action loop. The agent repeats an invalid action and receives the same failure feedback until the step budget runs out. (b) Repetitive reasoning loop. The agent’s reasoning ignores the current observation, and the agent cycles between the fridge and the microwave without completing the task. In both cases the agent’s internal state diverges from the environment dynamics, and the looping steps consume interaction budget while revealing no new observation. These are the steps our intrinsic reward penalizes. A natural way to improve exploration is to encourage the agent to visit a broader range of states. In principle, increasing the entropy of the explored state space can improve coverage, reduce mode collapse, and expose the agent to more informative trajectories. However, directly maximizing exploration entropy can also be problematic. If encouraged too strongly, the agent may drift toward diverse but task-irrelevant behavior, thereby sacrificing progress on the underlying objective. In long-horizon environments, this tension between exploration and exploitation is especially important: exploration should broaden the agent’s experience, but it should not pull the policy away from useful action sequences that lead to task completion. This paper pursues productive exploration through intrinsic curiosity-driven rewards , with a conservative formulation that preserves task alignment. Rather than positively rewarding state-space entropy increase, we penalize any step whose observation has already appeared in the episode. The intuition is that unhelpful actions, such as invalid steps or redundant repetitions, consume interaction budget and policy probability without revealing anything new about the environment. They can be detected simply by checking whether each new observation adds any new information to the agent’s memory. Our formulation reframes entropy increase as a consequence of avoiding unproductive actions rather than as an objective to be optimized directly. The penalty improves within-episode state-space coverage, while the task reward keeps exploration tied to task completion. We further formalize this argument by showing that the cumulative penalty measures how many distinct observations an episode visits, and that it bounds the episode’s visitation entropy (Section 3 ). A single-step analysis further shows that novel observations always increase entropy, while revisits of frequent observations decrease it. Our approach is consistent with the broader literature on intrinsic motivation in reinforcement learning, where curiosity, novelty seeking, and uncertainty reduction have been used to improve learning under sparse rewards Chentanez et al. (2004) ; Aubret et al. (2019) ; Gao et al. (2025) . It also aligns with recent efforts to train long-horizon LLM agents, where robustness depends not only on reasoning ability but also on the capacity to avoid repetitive or uninformative interactions with the environment Kalyan and Andrews (2025) . Within this setting, penalizing unhelpful actions provides a simple compromise between unrestricted entropy maximization and overly conservative exploitation. The resulting behavior promotes broader state coverage without losing contact with the task. In summary, we propose a conditional intrinsic reward framework that supports productive exploration by penalizing actions that yield no new informative observation. Our key argument is that entropy expansion is useful, but only when it is induced indirectly through the suppression of redundant or uninformative behavior. This allows the agent to explore more broadly while maintaining a strong coupling to task progress. We evaluate our proposed exploration strategy on two prominent multi-turn benchmark environments: ALFWorld and WebShop . Empirical results show that our approach surpasses recent baselines in performance metrics of success rates and significantly mitigates both invalid and repetitive action rates. 2 Related Work 2.1 Prompting-Based LLM Agents Early LLM agent frameworks rely on prompting for multi-step reasoning and action selection without updating model weights. ReAct Yao et al. (2023) interleaves reasoning (Thought) and actions (Act), outperforming pure reasoning or action prompting on tasks such as ALFWorld and WebShop. Reflexion Shinn et al. (2023) extends this with verbal reinforcement, storing self-reflections from failed episodes in episodic memory to guide future decisions. Although ReAct and Reflexion improve performance on multi-turn tasks, both methods depend heavily on self-evaluation quality, which degrades for smaller LLMs, and cannot structurally suppress invalid actions since prompting alone cannot alter action priors. 2.2 Reinforcement Learning for LLM Agents Recently, reinforcement learning (RL) has emerged as a principled approach for post-training LLMs, with growing focus on agent-based LLMs in multi-turn environments. PPO Schulman et al. (2017) and its critic-free variant GRPO Shao et al. (2024) , which estimates baselines from group rollout scores, are widely adopted for RL-based LLM training. RLOO Kool et al. (2019) ; Ahmadian et al. (2024) further reduces variance without a learned critic, and AGILE Feng et al. (2024) applies PPO to LLM agents using a four-module architecture with proactive expert consultation, significantly outperforming prompting on long-horizon QA tasks. Retrospex Xiang et al. (2024) combines an offline RL critic with LLM action likelihood through dynamic rescoring, improving performance on ALFWorld and WebShop over prompting baselines. GiGPO Feng et al. (2025) captures global trajectory quality and group-level effectiveness without additional rollouts, providing rich signals for LLM agent learning. Recently, ProxMO Fang et al. (2026) presents a framework to address GRPO’s context-agnostic normalization and GiGPO’s discrete state-grouping limitation. They explore the provision of gradient intensities based on task difficulty, and replace hard boundary partitioning with continuous semantic similarity weighting, so as to provide richer reward signals that are less task-agnostic. In totality, these works establish multiple avenues to improve vanilla RL for multi-turn LLM agents, such as stable baselines and supporting tools to provide more information about the world. However, they do not directly address the exploration failure modes we identify in this work. Specifically, we explore the notion of invalid actions that arise from environment precondition mismatches, resulting in action loops driven by high-confidence but unproductive behaviors. Our approach adds a conditional intrinsic reward that explicitly penalizes such behaviors during RL training. Recent RL methods for multi-turn LLM agents focus on improving credit assignment, exploration, and training stability. ArCHer Zhou and Zanette (2024) introduces a hierarchical RL framework combining off-policy temporal difference learning at the utterance level with on-policy policy gradients at the token level, substantially improving sample efficiency over PPO while emphasizing information-seeking behavior in multi-turn settings. Tree-GRPO Ji et al. (2026) improves training efficiency by replacing chain-based rollouts with tree-structured sampling, enabling step-level supervision from outcome rewards alone. Addressing exploration instability, EPO Xu et al. (2025) identifies exploration-exploitation cascade failure in shared multi-turn policies and mitigates it via trajectory-level entropy regularization and entropy smoothing, yielding gains on ScienceWorld and ALFWorld. Similarly, RAGEN Wang et al. (2025) studies multi-turn RL failure modes, identifying an “Echo Trap” caused by reward variance cliffs and gradient spikes, and proposes trajectory filtering with a critic for stabilization. While these works improve how agents learn—through efficient credit propagation, entropy stabilization, or robust optimization—our approach is complementary, focusing on what to explore by penalizing invalid or repetitive actions that fail to expand state-space knowledge, without itself performing credit assignment across turns. 2.3 Intrinsic Motivation and Exploration in RL Intrinsic motivation has long been used to improve exploration under sparse rewards by encouraging state diversity and novelty. Curiosity-based methods like Pathak et al. (2017) ; Burda et al. (2019) reward novel states or high prediction errors, while count-based exploration formalizes revisitation penalties through information gain via KL-divergence between prior and posterior state beliefs ( Bellemare et al., 2016 ) . Extending state-entropy exploration to task-reward settings, Kim et al. (2023) propose value-conditional state entropy (VCSE), addressing the tendency of naive entropy maximization to overexplore low-value regions by maximizing entropy within value partitions. Mutti et al. (2021) ; Ashlag et al. (2025) further provide a theoretical foundation for state entropy regularization, showing that it improves robustness and promotes broader coverage across multiple viable trajectories, unlike policy entropy which mainly injects noise along a dominant path. These works motivate our approach – by targeting state-space entropy, our conditional intrinsic penalty discourages revisiting already-observed states. Additionally, by tying the penalty to information gain rather than raw visitation counts, we ensure that only transitions that fail to expand the agent’s knowledge are penalized, preserving the pull of the task reward toward goal-relevant states. In LLM-based RL, intrinsic signals have recently been explored to complement sparse task rewards. MIRA Nourzad and Joe-Wong (2026) improves exploration by using memory graphs from agent trajectories and semantic reasoning to shape PPO advantages, mitigating poor early critic calibration. Similarly, our approach leverages accumulated experience for exploration, but instead defines an information-gain-based intrinsic signal that penalizes observations failing to expand state knowledge. This is simpler to compute, and is motivated by Shannon entropy (Proposition 2 ), while being aligned with repetitive and invalid behaviors in text-based environments. Further recent work on moral intrinsic rewards Tennant et al. (2025) has shown that intrinsic signals can shape agent behavior toward desired norms without task-specific reward engineering, reinforcing the broader applicability of intrinsic motivation for LLM alignment. Our contribution fits within this emerging direction: intrinsic rewards as a practical mechanism for shaping LLM agent behavior in ways that extrinsic rewards alone cannot achieve. 3 Methodology 3.1 Problem Setup We consider reinforcement learning for LLM agents operating in partially observable, long-horizon interactive environments. At each timestep t t , the agent is in state s t s_{t} , takes an action a t ∈ 𝒜 a_{t}\in\mathcal{A} , and receives an observation o t o_{t} from the environment. We define the agent’s state s t s_{t} as the set of all observations received so far along the trajectory, i.e., the information the agent has accumulated about the environment up to time t t . The objective is to learn a policy π ⁡ ( a t ∣ s t ) \pi(a_{t}\mid s_{t}) that maximizes expected cumulative reward while completing the task within a finite horizon T T . Unlike standard short-horizon decision problems, this setting introduces two recurring failure modes. First, the agent may produce invalid actions whose preconditions are not satisfied, causing the transition to fail or yielding no meaningful progress. Second, the agent may enter action loops , repeatedly selecting a small set of actions that do not improve task state or move the agent closer to completion. Both issues reduce learning efficiency and often reflect an imperfect internal model of the environment dynamics. In practice, these failures are especially harmful in LLM agents because they waste interaction budget and reinforce unproductive behavior patterns. 3.2 State Representation To support long-horizon decision making, we define the agent’s state as the accumulated observation history: s t = { o 1 , o 2 , … , o t } . s_{t}=\{o_{1},o_{2},\dots,o_{t}\}. This representation captures the information available to the agent at time t t . Instead of relying only on the most recent observation, the agent maintains a memory of the full trajectory of unique observations , enabling it to reason about what has already been explored and what remains uncertain. This accumulated state serves as the basis for evaluating whether a new observation provides additional information about the environment. At each step, the agent observes the current state s t s_{t} , selects an action a t a_{t} , and receives the next observation o t + 1 o_{t+1} . The state is then updated by appending the new observation: s t + 1 = s t ∪ { o t + 1 } . s_{t+1}=s_{t}\cup\{o_{t+1}\}. The intrinsic reward is computed from the change in information content between s t s_{t} and o t + 1 o_{t+1} . If the new observation does not improve the agent’s knowledge of the environment, a negative intrinsic reward is assigned. This signal is combined with the task reward and used to update the policy. 3.3 Conditional State-Space Exploration We propose a conditional state-space exploration mechanism that penalizes unhelpful transitions. After taking action a t a_{t} , the agent receives a new observation o t + 1 o_{t+1} , and the information gain is computed by comparing this new observation with the previous state s t s_{t} . Let I ⁡ ( ⋅ ) I(\cdot) denote a measure of information content or entropy associated with the agent’s accumulated state representation. We define the change in information as Δ ​ I ​ ( s t , o t + 1 ) = I ⁡ ( s t ∪ { o t + 1 } ) − I ⁡ ( s t ) . \Delta I(s_{t},o_{t+1})=I(s_{t}\cup\{o_{t+1}\})-I(s_{t}). This quantity measures whether the new observation expands the agent’s knowledge of the environment. The intrinsic reward is then defined as: r t intrinsic = { − γ if ​ Δ ​ I ​ ( s t , o t + 1 ) ≤ 0 , 0 otherwise , r_{t}^{\text{intrinsic}}=\begin{cases}-\gamma&\text{if }\Delta I(s_{t},o_{t+1})\leq 0,\\ 0&\text{otherwise},\end{cases} (1) where γ > 0 \gamma>0 controls the penalty magnitude. This formulation penalizes actions that do not lead to a meaningful increase in the agent’s information about the environment, thereby discouraging redundant or cyclic behavior. An overly strong incentive for novelty may lead the policy to explore diverse but irrelevant trajectories. By contrast, penalizing non-informative actions creates a task-constrained pressure toward visiting more distinct observations within an episode. The policy is discouraged from remaining in low-diversity action cycles, but it is still constrained by the external task reward, which ensures that exploration remains useful for task completion. This conditional structure is especially important in long-horizon environments, where the agent must balance exploration and exploitation over many sequential decisions. Actions that expand state coverage or contribute to task progress receive no intermediate positive incentive. However, actions that actively fail to improve the agent’s state knowledge are penalized . As a result, the learned policy is pushed toward trajectories that are both diverse and productive. This penalization mechanism encourages productive exploration by discouraging repeated observations and promoting broader coverage of the agent’s experience. We introduced a conditional state-space exploration framework driven by an information-aware intrinsic reward. Instead of directly maximizing unconstrained state entropy, which risks driving the agent toward task-irrelevant trajectories, our approach reframes exploration by penalizing actions that produce redundant state information. Our experimental evaluation demonstrates that this framework achieves substantial performance gains and significantly mitigates action repetition and circular reasoning patterns. Limitations Our experiments are conducted primarily on smaller reasoning models. Because exploration strategies are inherently influenced by a model’s overall capacity and pre-trained priors, larger instruction-tuned models may exhibit fewer failures than those documented in this study. Growth in model scale often mitigates baseline reasoning bottlenecks; nevertheless, optimizing smaller models remains highly valuable. Enhancing the capabilities of these smaller architectures enables more practical, targeted applications, particularly in hardware-constrained environments where deployment efficiency is critical. Additionally, this work focuses specifically on text-based environments within ALFWorld and WebShop, which feature relatively small, well-defined action spaces that lend themselves well to set representations. Environments with larger, continuous, or stochastic action spaces may exhibit vastly different dynamics under this set-based state representation, potentially limiting direct generalizability. Regardless of these limitations, our approach provides a structurally sound framework for agent reasoning and state representation in multi-turn settings. Ultimately, the insights gained from our set-based representation and reward design establish a foundation for future scaling and adaptation across more complex, open-ended environments. Appendix A Appendix A.1 Datasets: ALFWorld. ALFWorld ( Shridhar et al., 2020 ) is a text-based interactive environment designed for studying embodied decision making and long-horizon reasoning in language agents. Derived from the ALFRED benchmark, it converts household manipulation tasks into a partially observable textual setting where agents interact through natural language actions and observations. Tasks typically involve navigation, object manipulation, and sequential planning over multiple turns, making the environment particularly suitable for evaluating reinforcement learning methods for LLM agents under sparse rewards and delayed feedback. Concretely, ALFWorld contains 6 task types of various difficulty. The tasks are: • Pick & Place: agent must find an object of a specified type, pick it up, find the correct location to place it, and place it down there. • Examine in Light: agent must find an object of a specified type, locate and turn on a light source with the object still in hand. • Clean & Place: agent must find an object of a specified type, pick it up, move to a sink or a basin, turn on the faucet and wash the object, find the correct location to place it, and place it down there. • Heat & Place: agent must find an object of a specified type, pick it up, move to the microwave, heat the object by turning on the microwave, find the correct location to place it, and place it down there. • Cool & Place: agent must find an object of a specified type, pick it up, move to the fridge, place the object in the fridge to cool it, find the correct location to place it, and place it down there. • Pick Two & Place: agent must find an object of a specified type, find the correct location to place it, place it down there, look for another object of a specified type, pick up the object, return to the previous location, place it down there together with the first object. WebShop. WebShop ( Yao et al., 2022 ) is an e-commerce interaction benchmark that evaluates language agents on realistic online shopping tasks. In this environment, agents must search through large collections of products, inspect item descriptions and reviews, and iteratively refine decisions to satisfy user instructions. Unlike embodied environments, WebShop emphasizes retrieval, preference understanding, and multi-step reasoning in semi-structured web settings. The benchmark is widely used for evaluating the effectiveness of sequential decision-making and reinforcement learning approaches for interactive LLM agents. Concretely, the WebShop dataset contains 1,000,000 products, 670 unique attributes, 842,849 unique options, extracted publicly from Amazon. It presents over 12,000 annotated trajectories and an action space of 8 valid actions.
